CALIFORNIA DAILY/WEEKLY OVERTIME PAY CALCULATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS OVERTIME PAY-RATE INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet states California's general daily and weekly overtime and double-time pay-rate rules under Labor Code sections 510 and 511, and explains how the "regular rate of pay" used to compute overtime is determined. It is provided by Acme, Inc. to Jordan Lee for informational purposes. It states the baseline rule that applies to most nonexempt California employees; it does not itself classify any employee as exempt or nonexempt, does not address the separate statutory overtime formulas that apply to agricultural occupations or to personal attendants under the Domestic Worker Bill of Rights, does not describe the exemption for certain computer software employees, and does not walk through the election procedure by which an employer and its employees may adopt an alternative workweek schedule — each of those topics is addressed in a separate document.

DAILY OVERTIME AND DOUBLE-TIME TRIGGERS
Labor Code section 510(a) states that eight hours of labor constitutes a day's work. Under the statute's general rule, work in excess of eight hours in one workday is compensated at no less than one and one-half times the employee's regular rate of pay, up through 12 hours in that workday. Work in excess of 12 hours in one workday is compensated at no less than twice the employee's regular rate of pay. These daily thresholds apply independently of, and in addition to, the weekly overtime threshold and the seventh-consecutive-day premium the same subdivision also states.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Any work in excess of eight hours in one workday and any work in excess of 40 hours in any one workweek and the first eight hours worked on the seventh day of work in any one workweek shall be compensated at the rate of no less than one and one-half times the regular rate of pay for an employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 510(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=510.)
  "Any work in excess of 12 hours in one day shall be compensated at the rate of no less than twice the regular rate of pay for an employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 510(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=510.)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, section 510(a); it is not corroborated by an independent second source. Section 510(a) itself states that its daily-overtime requirements do not apply to an employee working under an alternative workweek schedule adopted under section 511, under a collective-bargaining alternative workweek schedule under section 514, or under section 554; this document addresses that alternative-workweek cross-reference in a separate clause below rather than repeating it here. This document does not address the separate, different daily/weekly overtime thresholds that other statutes set for agricultural occupations, personal attendants, or other categories carved out elsewhere in this corpus.

WEEKLY OVERTIME TRIGGER (OVER 40 HOURS)
Separately from the daily overtime threshold, Labor Code section 510(a) also requires that any work in excess of 40 hours in a single workweek be compensated at no less than one and one-half times the employee's regular rate of pay. This weekly threshold operates on its own: an employee who works no more than eight hours on any single day, but more than 40 hours across the workweek, is entitled to overtime pay for the hours over 40 even though no individual workday exceeded the daily threshold. Section 510 does not itself define "workweek"; a workweek is a fixed and regularly recurring period of seven consecutive days that an employer establishes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Any work in excess of eight hours in one workday and any work in excess of 40 hours in any one workweek and the first eight hours worked on the seventh day of work in any one workweek shall be compensated at the rate of no less than one and one-half times the regular rate of pay for an employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 510(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=510.)
  Known gap: The core statutory quote for the weekly threshold is drawn from the same sentence of section 510(a) already quoted in this document's daily-triggers clause; it is not an independent source. This document does not independently trace the definition of "workweek" to a specific statutory or wage-order provision beyond the general concept stated above; that concept is treated here as background context rather than as a citation-verified rule with its own quoted source.

SEVENTH-CONSECUTIVE-DAY PREMIUM
Labor Code section 510(a) sets a separate premium for the seventh consecutive day of work in a workweek. The first eight hours worked on the seventh consecutive day of work in a workweek are compensated at no less than one and one-half times the employee's regular rate of pay. Any work beyond eight hours on that seventh consecutive day is compensated at no less than twice the employee's regular rate of pay. This premium is tied to the seventh consecutive day of work within a single workweek, not to the seventh calendar day of any period, and applies in addition to the separate daily and weekly overtime thresholds the same subdivision states.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Any work in excess of eight hours in one workday and any work in excess of 40 hours in any one workweek and the first eight hours worked on the seventh day of work in any one workweek shall be compensated at the rate of no less than one and one-half times the regular rate of pay for an employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 510(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=510.)
  "In addition, any work in excess of eight hours on any seventh day of a workweek shall be compensated at the rate of no less than twice the regular rate of pay of an employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 510(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=510.)
  Known gap: Both quoted provisions come from the same statutory subdivision, section 510(a); they are not independent sources of one another. This document does not address the separate day-of-rest statute (Labor Code section 551 and related provisions) governing an employee's entitlement to one day of rest in seven, which is a distinct legal question from the overtime premium described in this clause and is addressed, where covered, in a separate document.

NO STACKING OF OVERTIME RATES, AND THE ALTERNATIVE WORKWEEK CROSS-REFERENCE
Labor Code section 510(a) states that nothing in the section requires an employer to combine more than one rate of overtime compensation to calculate the amount owed for a single hour of overtime work — that is, the same hour of work is not stacked with more than one premium multiplier. Section 510(a) also states that its daily/weekly overtime requirements do not apply to an employee working under an alternative workweek schedule adopted under Labor Code section 511, under a collective-bargaining alternative workweek schedule adopted under section 514, or under a schedule to which the general overtime chapter is inapplicable under section 554. Section 511, in turn, allows the employees of an employer to adopt a regularly scheduled alternative workweek authorizing up to 10 hours of work per day within a 40-hour workweek without a daily overtime premium for those scheduled hours, but only through a specific statutory procedure: a proposal is deemed adopted only if it is approved by a secret-ballot election in which at least two-thirds of the affected employees in a readily identifiable work unit vote in favor.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Nothing in this section requires an employer to combine more than one rate of overtime compensation in order to calculate the amount to be paid to an employee for any hour of overtime work."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 510(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=510.)
  "An alternative workweek schedule adopted pursuant to Section 511."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 510(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=510.)
  "Upon the proposal of an employer, the employees of an employer may adopt a regularly scheduled alternative workweek that authorizes work by the affected employees for no longer than 10 hours per day within a 40-hour workweek without the payment to the affected employees of an overtime rate of compensation pursuant to this section."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 511(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=511.)
  "A proposal to adopt an alternative workweek schedule shall be deemed adopted only if it receives approval in a secret ballot election by at least two-thirds of affected employees in a readily identifiable work unit."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 511(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=511.)
  Known gap: This document describes the existence of the section 511 alternative-workweek-schedule mechanism and its two-thirds secret-ballot election requirement only as background for understanding section 510(a)'s cross-reference; it does not independently walk through the full election procedure (the pre-election disclosure requirement, the reporting requirement, repeal mechanics, or anti-coercion protections), which is addressed in a separate document in this corpus. The quoted no-stacking sentence and the quoted alternative-workweek cross-reference both come from section 510(a); the two section 511(a) quotes both come from section 511(a); within each pair the sources are not independent of one another.

WHAT COUNTS AS THE "REGULAR RATE OF PAY"
Overtime and double-time premiums under Labor Code section 510 are calculated as multiples of an employee's "regular rate of pay," a term the statute uses but does not itself define. The state agency responsible for enforcing California's wage and hour laws describes the regular rate of pay as the compensation an employee normally earns for the work performed, which can include hourly earnings, salary, piecework earnings, commissions, and certain bonuses — not only a stated hourly wage. When a nondiscretionary bonus is paid as compensation for hours worked, production, proficiency, or as an incentive to remain employed, it is included in determining the regular rate of pay used to compute overtime. When an employee is paid two or more different hourly rates by the same employer during a single workweek, the regular rate of pay for that workweek is a weighted average, calculated by dividing total earnings for the workweek (including earnings during overtime hours) by the total hours worked during the workweek (including the overtime hours).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A nondiscretionary bonus is included in determining the regular rate of pay for computing overtime when the bonus is compensation for hours worked, production or proficiency, or as an incentive to remain employed by the same employer."
  — Cal. Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, Overtime FAQ, DIR, DLSE FAQ: Overtime (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/faq_overtime.htm)
  "If you are paid two or more rates by the same employer during the workweek , the regular rate is the "weighted average" which is determined by dividing your total earnings for the workweek, including earnings during overtime hours, by the total hours worked during the workweek, including the overtime hours."
  — Cal. Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, Overtime FAQ, DIR, DLSE FAQ: Overtime (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/faq_overtime.htm)
  Known gap: This clause relies on published guidance from the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (DLSE), a state enforcement agency, rather than on statutory text or a wage order provision defining "regular rate of pay" directly — this document did not locate a Labor Code section or IWC Wage Order section that itself defines the term for general nonexempt employees; the concept has instead developed through agency guidance and California case law (see the following clause on flat-sum bonuses). DLSE guidance documents such as this one are not themselves regulations adopted through the formal rulemaking procedure of the Administrative Procedure Act, and a California appellate case has held that at least one prior DLSE enforcement policy on a related overtime-calculation question was void for that reason; this document treats the quoted DLSE guidance as the agency's current published interpretation, not as binding law with the force of a statute or a properly promulgated regulation. This clause's two citations are drawn from different questions within the same DLSE FAQ page rather than from two independent publications.

FLAT-SUM BONUSES: THE DIVISOR USED TO COMPUTE THE REGULAR RATE
The California Supreme Court has addressed how to convert a flat sum bonus earned during a single pay period into a per-hour value for purposes of calculating overtime pay. In Alvarado v. Dart Container Corp. of California (2018) 4 Cal.5th 542, the court considered three candidate divisors for that per-hour value: the number of hours the employee actually worked during the pay period (including overtime hours); the number of nonovertime hours the employee worked during the pay period; or the number of nonovertime hours that exist in the pay period regardless of hours actually worked. The court held that the correct divisor is the number of nonovertime hours the employee actually worked during the pay period — not the larger total that would include overtime hours. Dividing by a smaller, nonovertime-hours-only denominator produces a higher per-hour value for the bonus, and therefore a higher overtime premium, than dividing by total hours worked would produce.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "we decide how an employee’s overtime pay rate should be calculated when the employee has earned a flat sum bonus during a single pay period. Specifically, we consider whether the divisor for purposes of calculating the per-hour value of the bonus should be (1) the number of hours the employee actually worked during the pay period, including overtime hours; (2) the number of nonovertime hours the employee worked during the pay period; or (3) the number of nonovertime hours that exist in the pay period, regardless of the number of hours the employee actually worked. We conclude that the divisor should be the second of these options."
  — Alvarado v. Dart Container Corp. of California, 4 Cal.5th 542 (2018) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4474533/alvarado-v-dart-container-corp-of-california/)
  Known gap: This clause is based on one appellate decision (a published California Supreme Court opinion), corroborated only by state agency guidance describing a similar divisor rule for flat-sum bonuses (quoted in the preceding clause's gap discussion, not repeated here as a separate citation), not by a second independent judicial decision. The Alvarado opinion itself notes that the agency guidance it discusses was, at the time, a DLSE enforcement-policy-manual position that had not been adopted through formal rulemaking, and the court reached its holding through its own interpretation of the governing statutes and wage order rather than by deferring to that manual. This document did not research whether later legislation or case law has modified Alvarado's specific holding. Alvarado addressed a flat sum bonus paid during a single pay period to an hourly employee; it does not by itself resolve every possible bonus, commission, or piece-rate regular-rate scenario, and this document does not attempt to catalog those other scenarios beyond the general description in the preceding clause.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
By signing below, Jordan Lee acknowledges having received and reviewed this information sheet describing California's general daily and weekly overtime and double-time pay-rate rules.

Company: Acme, Inc.

Employee signature date: September 1, 2026

Signed at: Oakland, California
